claim: All light-gated ion channels, including red-shifted channelrhodopsins (ChRs), are activated by blue light.
source: A well-known phenomenon in the optogenetic toolbox is that all light-gated ion channels, including red-shifted channelrhodopsins (ChRs), are activated by blue light, whereas blue-shifted ChRs are minimally responsive to longer wavelengths.
evidence: This is stated as a well-known phenomenon in the field, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Blue-shifted ChRs are minimally responsive to longer wavelengths.
source: A well-known phenomenon in the optogenetic toolbox is that all light-gated ion channels, including red-shifted channelrhodopsins (ChRs), are activated by blue light, whereas blue-shifted ChRs are minimally responsive to longer wavelengths.
evidence: This is stated as a well-known phenomenon in the field, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: The system allows high-frequency activation of neurons with pulses of red light.
source: Here, we took advantage of this feature to create a system which allows high-frequency activation of neurons with pulses of red light, while permitting the suppression of action potentials (APs) with millisecond precision by blue light.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The system permits the suppression of action potentials (APs) with millisecond precision by blue light.
source: Here, we took advantage of this feature to create a system which allows high-frequency activation of neurons with pulses of red light, while permitting the suppression of action potentials (APs) with millisecond precision by blue light.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The system was achieved by pairing an ultrafast red-shifted ChR with a blue light-sensitive anion channel of appropriately matching kinetics.
source: We achieved this by pairing an ultrafast red-shifted ChR with a blue light-sensitive anion channel of appropriately matching kinetics.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: Creating the system required screening several anion-selective ChRs.
source: This required screening several anion-selective ChRs, followed by a model-based mutagenesis strategy to optimize their kinetics and light spectra.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: Creating the system required a model-based mutagenesis strategy to optimize kinetics and light spectra.
source: This required screening several anion-selective ChRs, followed by a model-based mutagenesis strategy to optimize their kinetics and light spectra.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: Slice electrophysiology in the hippocampus demonstrates minimal excitation from blue light.
source: Slice electrophysiology in the hippocampus as well as behavioral inspection of vibrissa movement demonstrate a minimal excitation from blue light.
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Behavioral inspection of vibrissa movement demonstrates minimal excitation from blue light.
source: Slice electrophysiology in the hippocampus as well as behavioral inspection of vibrissa movement demonstrate a minimal excitation from blue light.
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The system allows high-frequency optogenetic excitation of neurons with red light.
source: Of significant potential value, in contrast to existing tools, the system we introduce here allows high-frequency optogenetic excitation of neurons with red light, while blue light suppression of APs is confined within the duration of the light pulse.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Blue light suppression of APs is confined within the duration of the light pulse.
source: Of significant potential value, in contrast to existing tools, the system we introduce here allows high-frequency optogenetic excitation of neurons with red light, while blue light suppression of APs is confined within the duration of the light pulse.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Optical manipulation of neuronal activity has become an indispensable tool in studies for functional analysis of brain circuits.
source: Despite the short history of optogenetics, optical manipulation of neuronal activity has become an indispensable tool in the studies for functional analysis of brain circuits.
evidence: This is a statement about the field of optogenetics, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Current excitatory opsins show light sensitivity ranging from near UV to near far-red spectra.
source: Main development among these expansions is the discovery of opsins of diverse excitation spectra, with the current excitatory opsins showing light sensitivity ranging from near UV to near far-red spectra (Yizhar et al., 2011; Deisseroth and Hegemann, 2017; Marshel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: All opsins, in addition to their own excitation spectral peak, are activated by blue light.
source: A major concern in the use of opsins with longer excitation spectra is that all opsins, in addition to their own excitation spectral peak, are activated by blue light, a problem known in the field as cross-talk or bleed-through.
evidence: This is stated as a major concern in the field, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: The problem of all opsins being activated by blue light is known in the field as cross-talk or bleed-through.
source: A major concern in the use of opsins with longer excitation spectra is that all opsins, in addition to their own excitation spectral peak, are activated by blue light, a problem known in the field as cross-talk or bleed-through.
evidence: This is stated as terminology used in the field.

claim: Attempts to create blue light-insensitive opsins will likely be unsuccessful due to the intrinsic blue absorption by the retinal molecule.
source: Attempts to create blue light-insensitive opsins will likely be unsuccessful due to the intrinsic blue absorption by the retinal molecule, the non-encoded chromophore, which captures light energy in channelrhodopsins (Waddell et al., 1973; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the chemical properties of retinal, supported by citations.

claim: The retinal molecule is the non-encoded chromophore which captures light energy in channelrhodopsins.
source: Attempts to create blue light-insensitive opsins will likely be unsuccessful due to the intrinsic blue absorption by the retinal molecule, the non-encoded chromophore, which captures light energy in channelrhodopsins (Waddell et al., 1973; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: One approach to overcome cross-talk uses a variant of blue-shifted ChR with fast kinetics in combination with a slow kinetics red-shifted ChR.
source: One uses a variant of blue-shifted ChR with fast kinetics in combination with a slow kinetics red-shifted ChR (R-ChR) (Klapoetke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The reasoning for using fast blue-shifted ChR with slow red-shifted ChR is that short pulses of blue light will activate only fast ChR.
source: The reasoning is that short pulses of blue light will activate only fast ChR.
evidence: This is an explanation of the rationale behind a published approach.

claim: The method using fast blue-shifted ChR with slow red-shifted ChR requires tight regulation of protein expression and light intensity.
source: Since it requires a tight regulation of the protein expression as well as the light intensity, this method has not been adopted for in vivo application.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of a published approach.

claim: The method using fast blue-shifted ChR with slow red-shifted ChR has not been adopted for in vivo application.
source: Since it requires a tight regulation of the protein expression as well as the light intensity, this method has not been adopted for in vivo application.
evidence: This is an inference about the adoption of a published approach.

claim: Another approach to overcome cross-talk is to expose axons expressing an R-ChR to prolonged photostimulation, during which axons become unresponsive to light pulses and cease to fire.
source: Another approach is to expose axons expressing an R-ChR to prolonged photostimulation, during which axons become unresponsive to light pulses and cease to fire (Hooks et al., 2015; Faress et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The prolonged photostimulation method is limited to axonal regions as prolonged optical stimulation of the soma induces trains of action potentials.
source: This method is limited to axonal regions as prolonged optical stimulation of the soma induces trains of action potentials (APs).
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of a published approach.

claim: Prolonged stimulation of the axons of neurons with slow spike-frequency adaptation may result in repetitive activity rather than depolarization block.
source: Additionally, prolonged stimulation of the axons of neurons with slow spike-frequency adaptation, such as fast-spiking interneurons, may result in repetitive activity rather than depolarization block (Hooks et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: A potential solution to the problem of cross-talk is to co-express a blue-shifted anion channelrhodopsin (B-ACR) along with the R-ChR to 'suppress' the excitation of R-ChR by blue light.
source: A potential solution to the problem of cross-talk is to co-express a blue-shifted anion channelrhodopsin (B-ACR) along with the R-ChR to 'suppress' the excitation of R-ChR by blue light.
evidence: This describes the conceptual approach of the study.

claim: A neuron co-expressing B-ACR and R-ChR would selectively produce APs to red light and not blue light.
source: The intention is to have a neuron co-expressing such opsins selectively produce APs to red light and not blue light.
evidence: This describes the intended outcome of the co-expression strategy.

claim: A recent study achieved co-expression of B-ACR and R-ChR by pairing GtACR2 and Chrimson.
source: A recent study achieved this, by pairing GtACR2 and Chrimson (Vierock et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The GtACR2 and Chrimson system is more suitable for optical manipulation of lower frequency stimulation due to its relatively slow kinetics.
source: Due to its relatively slow kinetics, this system is more suitable for optical manipulation of lower frequency stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of a published system.

claim: Optical activation of opsins with long opening lifetime may elevate the concentration of intracellular ions with unintended physiological complications.
source: Additionally, optical activation of these opsins, which have a long opening lifetime, may elevate the concentration of intracellular ions with unintended physiological complications (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential physiological effects.

claim: vfChrimson is currently the fastest R-ChR.
source: We chose vfChrimson – currently the fastest R-ChR – to gain precise temporal control of red-light excitation (Mager et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: ZipACR is an ultrafast blue light-activated chloride channel.
source: To generate a B-ACR with vfChrimson matching kinetics we used a model-based mutagenesis approach to modify the kinetic properties of ZipACR, an ultrafast blue light-activated chloride channel (Govorunova et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Due to the high intracellular chloride concentration in the axonal terminal, the use of a chloride channel-based expression system must be restricted to the somato-dendritic regions.
source: It must be noted that due to the high intracellular chloride concentration in the axonal terminal (Turecek and Trussell, 2001; Messier et al., 2018) the use of a chloride channel-based expression system must be restricted to the somato-dendritic regions (Mahn et al., 2016; Messier et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: ZipACR variants I151T and I151V display appropriate kinetics, light spectra, and photocurrent magnitudes for the co-expressing system.
source: We describe several variants of ZipACR, focusing on two, I151T and I151V, which display appropriate kinetics, light spectra, and photocurrent magnitudes for the purposes of our co-expressing system.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The optimized anion channels were paired with a membrane-trafficking optimized vfChrimson (IvfChr) in a single expression unit.
source: We then paired the optimized anion channels with a membrane-trafficking optimized vfChrimson (IvfChr) in a single expression unit.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: Zip-IvfChr, when expressed in neurons, can drive time-locked high-frequency APs in response to red pulses (635 nm).
source: The new system, Zip-IvfChr, when expressed in neurons, can drive time-locked high-frequency APs in response to red pulses (635 nm).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In response to blue pulses (470 nm), Zip-IvfChr produces no APs.
source: On the other hand, in response to blue pulses (470 nm), Zip-IvfChr produces no APs.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Blue light pulses transiently suppress APs in Zip-IvfChr-expressing neurons.
source: As expected, blue light pulses transiently suppress APs in Zip-IvfChr-expressing neurons, but the suppression is fully reversed within 5 ms after termination of light pulses due to the use of fast ZipACR mutants.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The suppression of APs by blue light in Zip-IvfChr-expressing neurons is fully reversed within 5 ms after termination of light pulses.
source: As expected, blue light pulses transiently suppress APs in Zip-IvfChr-expressing neurons, but the suppression is fully reversed within 5 ms after termination of light pulses due to the use of fast ZipACR mutants.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Zip-IvfChr activation by red but not blue light triggered vibrissa movement of large amplitudes when tested in the facial motor nucleus in the brainstem.
source: When tested in the facial motor nucleus in the brainstem, Zip-IvfChr activation by red but not blue light triggered vibrissa movement of large amplitudes.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Chrimson and its variants have the most red-shifted spectra.
source: The channelrhodopsin Chrimson and its variants have the most red-shifted spectra (Klapoetke et al., 2014), and their response to 470 nm has a slower on-rate compared to the 590 nm light (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A , B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and reference to figure data.

claim: Chrimson variants' response to 470 nm has a slower on-rate compared to the 590 nm light.
source: The channelrhodopsin Chrimson and its variants have the most red-shifted spectra (Klapoetke et al., 2014), and their response to 470 nm has a slower on-rate compared to the 590 nm light (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A , B).
evidence: This is supported by reference to figure data.

claim: Despite slower on-rate to 470 nm, 470 nm light is equally effective in inducing APs as 590 nm light for Chrimson variants.
source: Despite this, 470 nm light is equally effective in inducing APs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by reference to figure data.

claim: Co-expressing B-ACR variant GtACR2 along with a Chrimson variant would allow photostimulation of targeted neurons by red light to only activate R-ChR.
source: By co-expressing the B-ACR variant GtACR2, along with a Chrimson variant, photostimulation of targeted neurons by red light would be expected to only activate R-ChR, which causes photoactivation of these neurons.
evidence: This is an inference about the expected outcome of the co-expression strategy.

claim: Blue light activates both R-ChR and GtACR2 in co-expressing neurons.
source: Blue light, however, activates R-ChR as well as GtACR2.
evidence: This is an inference about the expected outcome of the co-expression strategy.

claim: The chloride channel induces shunting inhibition of the neurons which would prevent firing by blue light.
source: This allows the chloride channel to induce shunting inhibition of the neurons which in turn would be expected to prevent firing of the neurons by blue light (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an inference about the expected outcome of the co-expression strategy, illustrated in a figure.

claim: When Chrimson was co-expressed with tdTomato, illumination at 470 and 590 nm wavelengths led to similar amounts of courtship song in Drosophila.
source: When Chrimson was co-expressed with an inactive control protein (tdTomato), illumination at 470 and 590 nm wavelengths led to similar amounts of courtship song (110.1 ± 12.8 and 78.5 ± 11.6 pulses per 10 s, n = 16–17, respectively), demonstrating that blue light at the chosen intensity can efficiently activate Chrimson (Figure 1B3).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data in Drosophila.

claim: Blue light at the chosen intensity can efficiently activate Chrimson in Drosophila P1 neurons.
source: When Chrimson was co-expressed with an inactive control protein (tdTomato), illumination at 470 and 590 nm wavelengths led to similar amounts of courtship song (110.1 ± 12.8 and 78.5 ± 11.6 pulses per 10 s, n = 16–17, respectively), demonstrating that blue light at the chosen intensity can efficiently activate Chrimson (Figure 1B3).
evidence: This is an inference from experimental data in Drosophila.

claim: When Chrimson was co-expressed with GtACR2, 590 nm light illumination reliably elicited male courtship song in Drosophila.
source: When Chrimson was co-expressed with the blue-sensitive anion channelrhodopsin GtACR2, 590 nm light illumination reliably elicited male courtship song (95.2 ± 9.14 pulses per 10 s); while 470 nm light illumination did not evoke any detectable pulse song (n = 17–18).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data in Drosophila.

claim: When Chrimson was co-expressed with GtACR2, 470 nm light illumination did not evoke any detectable pulse song in Drosophila.
source: When Chrimson was co-expressed with the blue-sensitive anion channelrhodopsin GtACR2, 590 nm light illumination reliably elicited male courtship song (95.2 ± 9.14 pulses per 10 s); while 470 nm light illumination did not evoke any detectable pulse song (n = 17–18).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data in Drosophila.

claim: Neither 590 nor 470 nm light pulses exposure induced courtship song in flies expressing only GtACR2.
source: Neither 590 nor 470 nm light pulses exposure induced courtship song in flies expressing only GtACR2 (n = 5).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data in Drosophila.

claim: GtACR2 has slow current decay (161 ± 24 ms, n = 3).
source: Although GtACR2 proved to be effective in protocols with pulses of long duration, its slow current decay (Figure 2A, see GtACR2, 161 ± 24 ms, n = 3) limits its application to optical stimulations of lower frequencies (Govorunova et al., 2015; Govorunova et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data and supported by citations.

claim: GtACR2's slow current decay limits its application to optical stimulations of lower frequencies.
source: Although GtACR2 proved to be effective in protocols with pulses of long duration, its slow current decay (Figure 2A, see GtACR2, 161 ± 24 ms, n = 3) limits its application to optical stimulations of lower frequencies (Govorunova et al., 2015; Govorunova et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference from experimental data and supported by citations.

claim: vfChrimson can induce APs up to the intrinsic limit of the neurons.
source: For a fast R-ChR, we evaluated the recently published vfChrimson, the fastest red-shifted channelrhodopsin available at this time, which can induce APs up to the intrinsic limit of the neurons (Mager et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: IvfChr has a channel off-rate time constant of 5.6 ± 0.3 ms (n = 10).
source: In our measurements in HEK 293 cells, IvfChr has a channel off-rate consistent with previously reported (Mager et al., 2018) (off-rate time constant of 5.6 ± 0.3 ms, n = 10 compared to C-Chrimson-ts 21.5 ± 1.2 ms, n = 10; mean ± SEM, Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data in HEK 293 cells.

claim: C-Chrimson-ts has a channel off-rate time constant of 21.5 ± 1.2 ms (n = 10).
source: In our measurements in HEK 293 cells, IvfChr has a channel off-rate consistent with previously reported (Mager et al., 2018) (off-rate time constant of 5.6 ± 0.3 ms, n = 10 compared to C-Chrimson-ts 21.5 ± 1.2 ms, n = 10; mean ± SEM, Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data in HEK 293 cells.

claim: IvfChr has 40% reduction of photocurrent compared to C-ChrimsonR-ts.
source: When comparing C-ChrimsonR-ts and IvfChr photocurrents, we observe 40% reduction of photocurrent of IvfChr (0.086 ± 0.055 pA/pF/A.U., n = 25) compared to C-ChrimsonR-ts 0.145 ± 0.126 pA/pF/A.U., n = 25; mean ± SD, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B when the peak photocurrent amplitude was adjusted to membrane capacitance and membrane fluorescence.
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data in HEK 293 cells.

claim: ZipACR has an off-rate time constant of 9.5 ± 3.0 ms (n = 9).
source: ZipACR, although spectrally not ideal (~515 nm; Govorunova et al., 2017) has a kinetic close to the desired range (9.5 ± 3.0 ms, n = 9) and it has strong photocurrents (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data.

claim: ZipACR has strong photocurrents.
source: ZipACR, although spectrally not ideal (~515 nm; Govorunova et al., 2017) has a kinetic close to the desired range (9.5 ± 3.0 ms, n = 9) and it has strong photocurrents (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data.

claim: Individual pulses of 470 nm light resulted in time-locked suppression of APs in organotypic hippocampal neurons expressing ZipACR.
source: To test the inhibitory property of ZipACR, we injected 40 Hz somatic current in organotypic hippocampal neurons expressing the channel. Consistent with the original report, individual pulses of 470 nm light resulted in the time-locked suppression of APs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data in organotypic slices.

claim: In 8 out of ten cases, 470 nm light induced significantly fewer APs than 635 nm light in granule cells co-expressing ZipACR and vfChrimson.
source: Recordings from the granule cells in acute hippocampal slices co-expressing ZipACR and vfChrimson showed that, in 8 out of ten cases 470 nm light induced significantly fewer APs than 635 nm light (Figure 2C1), in line with our prediction.
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data in acute slices.

claim: Individual APs time-locked to the blue light offset were consistently observed in neurons co-expressing ZipACR and vfChrimson.
source: However, we consistently observed the appearance of individual APs time-locked to the blue light offset (Figure 2C1, C2).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data in acute slices.

claim: Due to the fast-closing rate, the photoinhibitory current generated by ZipACR decays too early to suppress the remaining excitatory response of vfChrimson.
source: We concluded that due to the fast-closing rate, the photoinhibitory current generated by ZipACR decays too early to suppress the remaining excitatory response of vfChrimson.
evidence: This is an inference from experimental observations.

claim: It is technically easier to generate mutations with slower kinetics and blue-shifted spectra than generating variants with faster on- and off-kinetics.
source: It is technically easier to generate mutations with slower kinetics and blue-shifted spectra than generating variants with faster on- and off-kinetics.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical feasibility of mutagenesis, drawing from knowledge.

claim: ZipACR was used as a template for further mutagenesis instead of modifying GtACR2.
source: Thus, we decided to use ZipACR as a template for further mutagenesis instead of further modifying GtACR2.
evidence: This describes the methodological decision made in the study.

claim: A homology model of ZipACR was generated with the crystal structure of GtACR1.
source: To identify relevant mutation sites in ZipACR, we generated a homology model of ZipACR with the crystal structure of GtACR1 (Govorunova et al., 2017) and identified the putative residues forming the retinal binding pocket in ZipACR (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: Multiple alignments were performed with GtACR1 and GtACR2 to identify possible replacement residues in ZipACR.
source: Multiple alignments were performed with the kinetically slower GtACR1 and GtACR2 to identify possible replacement of these residues that would result in slower kinetics and/or small blue-shift in ZipACR without disrupting the channel function (Figure 3A2).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: I151V and I151T variants of ZipACR have a small increase in channel off-rate time constant compared to the original ZipACR.
source: Of these candidates, we identified I151V and I151T at the fourth transmembrane domain of ZipACR that resulted in a small increase in channel off-rate time constant (15.5 ± 8.4 ms for I151V and 20.2 ± 6.4 ms for I151T, mean ± SD, Figure 3B) compared to the original ZipACR (9.5 ± 2.9 ms, mean ± SD).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data in HEK 293 cells.

claim: Neither Zip(151V) nor Zip(151T) mutations changed the ion permeability of ZipACR.
source: Neither Zip(151V) nor Zip(151T) mutations changed the ion permeability of ZipACR as measured by channel reversal potential in potassium gluconate and cesium chloride based intracellular recording solutions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data.

claim: Except in two instances, blue light pulses were consistently effective in blocking APs in neurons expressing Zip(151T), while red light had no effect on APs induction.
source: Except in two instances, blue light pulses were consistently effective in blocking APs, while red light had no effect on APs induction (Figure 3E, n = 10 for 470 and n = 6 for 635, the two outliers are presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data in hippocampal slices.

claim: ZipACR may produce light-evoked APs at resting or hyperpolarized membrane potentials.
source: It has been reported that at resting or hyperpolarized membrane potentials ZipACR may produce light-evoked APs (Kato et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Light-evoked APs by ZipACR at resting or hyperpolarized membrane potentials were not observed under the experimental setup used in this study.
source: We did not observe such a phenomenon under our experimental setup (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data.

claim: Co-injection of two viruses results in variability in the ratio of expression in different neurons.
source: Since co-injection of two viruses results in variability in the ratio of expression in different neurons, we used the bicistronic 2A approach (Supplementary material 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of co-injection, drawing from knowledge.

claim: The bicistronic 2A approach was favored over IRES and tandem fusion strategies.
source: We favored this system to the internal ribosomal entry sites (IRES) (Pelletier and Sonenberg, 1988; Douin et al., 2004) and tandem fusion strategies (Kleinlogel et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the methodological decision made in the study.

claim: IRES produces an unbalanced expression level with the second protein at much lower level.
source: As observed by us and reported by other groups, IRES produces an unbalanced expression level with the second protein at much lower level (Mizuguchi et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and the authors' observations.

claim: Testing of vfChrimson in the BiPOLES tandem fusion system with GtACR2 resulted in high levels of intracellular accumulation of the tandem opsins in HEK 293 cells.
source: The testing of vfChrimson in the recently published BiPOLES tandem fusion system with GtACR2 (Vierock et al., 2021) resulted in high levels of intracellular accumulation of the tandem opsins in HEK 293 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data in HEK 293 cells.

claim: The bicistronic 2A cassette ensures an equimolar translation of the two proteins from one mRNA.
source: This ensures an equimolar translation of the two proteins from one mRNA and soma enrichment of the opsins in neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of the 2A system, drawing from knowledge.

claim: The vfChrimson in the bicistronic 2A cassette led to ~2.7× higher photocurrent compared to BiPOLES.
source: In comparison to BiPOLES with vfChrimson, the vfChrimson in our bicistronic 2A cassette led to ~2.7× higher photocurrent (–7.57 ± 5.37 pA/pF in ZipV-IvfChr compared to –2.72 ± 1.33 pA/pF in BiPOLES, n = 14) when tested in identical conditions, consistent with the improved membrane trafficking observed with IvfChr (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data in HEK 293 cells.

claim: In IvfChr-expressing neurons, both 470 and 635 nm lights induced APs.
source: As expected, in IvfChr-expressing neurons, both 470 and 635 nm lights induced APs (n = 6).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data in hippocampal slices.

claim: In neurons expressing ZipT-IvfChr, 635 nm pulses were equally effective in driving APs as in IvfChr-expressing neurons.
source: In neurons expressing ZipT-IvfChr (Figure 4B), 635 nm pulses were equally effective in driving APs.
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data in hippocampal slices.

claim: In neurons expressing ZipT-IvfChr, 470 nm light only induced modest depolarization, which did not produce the threshold for AP induction.
source: On the other hand, 470 nm light only induced modest depolarization, which did not produce the threshold for AP induction (n = 5–12 for each opsin).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data in hippocampal slices.

claim: Co-illumination with 470 and 635 nm failed to generate AP in ZipT-IvfChr-expressing neurons, showing blue light effectively nullifies the depolarizing property of red light.
source: Similarly, co-illumination with 470 and 635 nm also failed to generate AP, showing blue light effectively nullifies the depolarizing property of red light (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data in hippocampal slices.

claim: In IvfChr-expressing neurons, 470 and 635 nm light-induced APs with light powers as low as 1 mW/mm2.
source: In IvfChr-expressing neurons 470 and 635 nm light-induced APs with light powers as low as 1 mW/mm2 (n = 10, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data in hippocampal slices.

claim: ZipT-IvfChr-expressing neurons produced APs only to 635 nm light stimulation.
source: In contrast, ZipT-IvfChr-expressing neurons produced APs only to 635 nm light stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), whereas 470 nm light powers as high as 10 mW/mm2 failed to induce APs (n = 7–8, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data in hippocampal slices.

claim: 470 nm light powers as high as 10 mW/mm2 failed to induce APs in ZipT-IvfChr-expressing neurons.
source: In contrast, ZipT-IvfChr-expressing neurons produced APs only to 635 nm light stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), whereas 470 nm light powers as high as 10 mW/mm2 failed to induce APs (n = 7–8, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data in hippocampal slices.

claim: Blue light-induced APs were occasionally observed with ZipV-IvfChr, which may be explained by its relatively faster closure rate.
source: As for ZipV-IvfChr, we occasionally observed blue light-induced APs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), which may be explained by its relatively faster closure rate (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data and an inference about the mechanism.

claim: A reduction in probability of AP upon successive optical stimulation specifically to 635 nm pulses was noticed in neurons expressing IvfChr.
source: In neurons expressing IvfChr, we noticed a reduction in probability of AP upon successive optical stimulation specifically to 635 nm pulses (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data in hippocampal slices.
